analysis.one_liner: Opens congressional primaries to all voters, restricts general elections to the top two finishers, and takes redistricting away from partisan control.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in any of the three committees it was sent to, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state to run congressional primaries on a single ballot that any voter could cast, no matter their party or lack of one. Only the top two vote-getters would advance to the general election, even if both belonged to the same party. It also would have made Election Day a paid day off for federal workers and required congressional district lines to be drawn by independent commissions that could not consider party advantage. It was introduced by Rep. John Delaney and three Democratic colleagues, referred to three House committees, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters: independent and unaffiliated voters could vote in primaries instead of being locked out by party-run nominating processes; all voters would get more competitive general elections, since districts drawn to favor one party would be replaced by commission-drawn lines and primaries could not be captured by a party's most ideological voters. Federal employees would get Election Day off.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, especially independents locked out of primaries

how_it_helps.text: Every voter in a state or district could vote in the congressional primary regardless of party registration, on a single ballot containing all candidates [S3].
The general election would be limited to the two candidates who got the most primary votes, regardless of party, so a district where one party dominates could still produce a real contest [S3].

Congressional redistricting after the 2020 census would have to be done by an independent state commission barred from using partisan or political considerations, with no single party controlling it [S3].
Election Day would be treated as a legal public holiday for federal employment, and the bill states Congress's view that private employers should give workers the day off to vote [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The two major political parties would lose control of congressional nominations, since they could no longer restrict primaries to registered party members and could not guarantee their chosen candidates a spot on the general-election ballot. Incumbent members of Congress would face primaries open to all voters and districts not drawn to protect them.
analysis.who_pays_short: The two major parties and incumbents

drawbacks.text: A top-two system can push minor-party candidates off the general-election ballot entirely, since only the two highest primary vote-getters appear, and can produce general elections between two members of the same party [S3].
The Election Day holiday applies only to federal employees; private-sector workers would get a day off only if their employers voluntarily follow the bill's nonbinding suggestion [S3].
The redistricting provisions defer to state law on how commissions are appointed and composed, so states could design commissions in ways that fall short of genuine independence [S3].
Candidates would keep the option to list a party preference on the ballot, so party labels would still shape voter choices even though the party no longer controls the primary [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core reforms are real: opening primaries and taking map-drawing away from partisan majorities would likely make more House races competitive and give independents a say. The design has weak spots: the holiday covers only federal workers, top-two rules can crowd out third parties, and the commission requirements leave states room to water them down. Weighing this honestly, the bill was a broad but somewhat loosely specified reform whose main obstacle was that it would weaken the party structures that decide who runs Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, sent to a Judiciary subcommittee two weeks later, and no committee ever held a markup or sent it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Delaney introduced the bill on June 21, 2017, joined by Reps. Yarmuth, Kilmer, and Polis [S3].
It was referred the same day to the Committees on House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary [S5].
On July 10, 2017, it was referred within Judiciary to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice [S5].
No further action appears in the record through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The two major parties and incumbent members of Congress, who keep closed primaries and party-drawn districts; no voter group gained anything from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The two major parties and incumbents

for.name: Rep. John Delaney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill combining open top-two primaries, an Election Day federal holiday, and independent redistricting commissions.

for.name: Reps. John Yarmuth, Derek Kilmer, and Jared Polis

against.name: House committees of jurisdiction (House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, Judiciary)
against.role: Committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded before the Congress ended.

against.name: House leadership of the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration, and under normal practice no bill moves without the committees or the Speaker's calendar process advancing it.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill and Republicans controlled the House committees where it stalled, but no vote or hearing record shows how members would have split on the merits.

industries.industry: The two major political parties and their state organizations
industries.note: The bill ends state-run party primaries as the gateway to congressional ballots and forbids any party from controlling redistricting commissions, removing two of the parties' main levers over who gets elected. Their interest in keeping the current system runs against voters who want open primaries and competitive districts.

Open primaries expose incumbents to every voter in their district, top-two rules allow same-party challengers, and commission-drawn maps would end districts engineered to protect incumbents. The bill targets exactly the advantages officeholders have written into election law for themselves.
